evt-salem-witch-trials.why: Salem Village was a divided Puritan farming community, split by bitter quarrels over its minister, Samuel Parris, whose own daughter and niece were among the first girls afflicted. Frontier wars with the French and their Native allies had stoked fear, and Massachusetts was in political limbo while it waited for a new royal charter.
evt-salem-witch-trials.impact: Governor William Phips shut down the special court in October 1692 as ministers such as Increase Mather condemned the use of spectral evidence. Judge Samuel Sewall later publicly apologised, compensation was paid to victims' families in 1711, and Arthur Miller's play The Crucible used the trials to attack McCarthyism in the 1950s.

evt-charles-i-executed.why: Charles had ruled for eleven years without Parliament, raising money through unpopular levies such as ship money, and his religious policies provoked war with Scotland. After losing the first Civil War he secretly allied with the Scots and started a second, so the army purged Parliament of members still willing to negotiate with him.
evt-charles-i-executed.impact: Within weeks the monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished and England was declared a Commonwealth, later ruled by Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector. After the Restoration, surviving regicides were hunted down and executed, but the trial had established that even a king could be held to account by his subjects.

evt-great-chicago-fire.why: Chicago had grown at astonishing speed and was built largely of wood, with timber houses, wooden pavements and even plank streets. The summer and autumn of 1871 had been exceptionally dry, and the city's firefighters were exhausted after battling a large blaze the night before. The fire started in a barn on DeKoven Street.
evt-great-chicago-fire.impact: The fire left around a hundred thousand people homeless and destroyed about a third of the city's property. Chicago brought in stricter building codes favouring fireproof materials, attracted ambitious architects to the rebuilding, and kept growing so quickly that its population passed one million by 1890.

evt-rosa-parks.why: Montgomery's buses forced Black passengers to sit at the back and give up seats to white riders when the front filled. Parks was secretary of the local NAACP branch, and activists had been looking for a strong test case since a teenager, Claudette Colvin, was arrested for the same refusal earlier that year.
evt-rosa-parks.impact: The boycott turned Martin Luther King Jr. into a national figure and inspired protests across the South, and it led to the founding of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957. Parks lost her job and moved to Detroit, and in 2005 she became the first woman to lie in honour in the US Capitol.

evt-jfk-assassination.why: Kennedy went to Texas to heal splits in the state's Democratic Party ahead of the 1964 election. His open-topped limousine was driven slowly through Dealey Plaza in Dallas. Oswald, a former Marine who had once defected to the Soviet Union, had taken a job at the book depository only weeks before.
evt-jfk-assassination.impact: The Warren Commission concluded in 1964 that Oswald had acted alone, though many Americans never accepted its findings. Johnson invoked Kennedy's memory to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964, presidential protection was overhauled, and the 25th Amendment later set out clear rules for replacing a president who dies or is incapacitated.

evt-mandela-released.why: By the late 1980s South Africa was battered by international sanctions, sporting boycotts, a weakening economy and years of unrest in the townships. Officials had been holding secret talks with Mandela in prison, and the end of the Cold War removed the government's claim that the ANC was a communist threat.
evt-mandela-released.impact: Years of tense negotiations followed, marked by serious political violence, and Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. The first elections open to all races were held in 1994, a Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined apartheid-era crimes, and a new constitution was adopted in 1996.

evt-soviet-flag-lowered.why: Gorbachev's policies of openness and reform had loosened the party's grip while the economy kept failing. The August coup collapsed in three days after Boris Yeltsin rallied resistance in Moscow, and in early December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed an agreement declaring that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist.
evt-soviet-flag-lowered.impact: Fifteen independent countries emerged from the union, and Russia took over the Soviet seat on the UN Security Council along with most of its nuclear arsenal. Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan later gave up the nuclear weapons left on their soil, while rapid market reforms brought severe hardship to millions during the 1990s.

evt-death-of-diana.why: Diana's separation and divorce from Prince Charles had made her one of the most photographed people on earth, and pictures of her private life sold for huge sums. After leaving the Ritz Hotel in Paris, her car crashed in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. The driver, Henri Paul, was later found to have been drinking.
evt-death-of-diana.impact: The Queen faced criticism for staying at Balmoral and returned to London to make a rare televised tribute. Elton John's reworked Candle in the Wind became one of the best-selling singles ever, and a 2008 inquest ruled that Diana had been unlawfully killed by grossly negligent driving by her chauffeur and the pursuing photographers.

evt-september-11.why: Osama bin Laden's al-Qaeda had declared war on the United States, angered by American troops in Saudi Arabia and US policy in the Middle East. It had already bombed two US embassies in East Africa in 1998 and the warship USS Cole in 2000. Several hijackers trained at American flight schools.
evt-september-11.impact: Nearly three thousand people were killed, the deadliest terrorist attack in history. The United States created the Department of Homeland Security, passed the Patriot Act and expanded surveillance, and the attacks were cited in the build-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Bin Laden was killed by US special forces in Pakistan in 2011.

evt-covid-pandemic-declared.why: The World Health Organization had declared a global health emergency at the end of January, but the virus spread silently through air travel before many cases were detected. By March large outbreaks had taken hold in Italy, Iran and South Korea, and cases were rising in more than a hundred countries.
evt-covid-pandemic-declared.impact: The pandemic triggered the deepest global recession since the Second World War and normalised remote working and online schooling. The WHO later estimated around fifteen million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021. Vaccines using messenger RNA were approved for the first time, and the WHO ended the emergency in May 2023.

bat-stirling-bridge.why: When Scotland's royal line died out in 1290, Edward I of England was invited to choose between rival claimants and demanded to be recognised as overlord. His chosen king, John Balliol, later rebelled, so Edward invaded in 1296, sacked Berwick and took the Stone of Scone. Wallace and Andrew Moray then led uprisings.
bat-stirling-bridge.impact: Moray died of his wounds soon afterwards, and Edward defeated Wallace at Falkirk in 1298. Wallace was captured in 1305 and executed in London, but the resistance he led passed to Robert the Bruce, who won at Bannockburn in 1314. England finally recognised Scottish independence in 1328.

bat-lexington-concord.why: After the Seven Years' War, Britain tried to tax its American colonies through measures such as the Stamp Act, provoking protests like the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts, closing Boston's harbour and putting Massachusetts under military rule, while colonists organised militias ready to turn out at a minute's notice.
bat-lexington-concord.impact: Thousands of militiamen besieged the British in Boston, and the Second Continental Congress created a Continental Army under George Washington. Bunker Hill followed in June, and the Declaration of Independence in 1776. Ralph Waldo Emerson later called the first shot at Concord the shot heard round the world.

bat-borodino.why: Tsar Alexander I had broken with Napoleon's Continental System and resumed trade with Britain. In June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia with an army of more than 400,000 men, but the Russians kept retreating and burning supplies. Under pressure not to give up Moscow without a fight, Kutuzov finally stood his ground at Borodino.
bat-borodino.impact: Napoleon waited in Moscow for five weeks for a peace offer that never came. The destruction of his army encouraged Prussia and then Austria to join a new coalition, which beat him at Leipzig in 1813 and forced his abdication in 1814. Tchaikovsky later celebrated the Russian victory in his 1812 Overture.

bat-antietam.why: Fresh from victory at the Second Battle of Bull Run, Robert E. Lee invaded Maryland hoping a win on Union soil would bring European recognition for the Confederacy. Union soldiers then found a copy of Lee's orders wrapped around some cigars, revealing that his army was divided, and George McClellan moved to attack.
bat-antietam.impact: It remains the bloodiest single day in American history. Britain and France held back from recognising the Confederacy, and emancipation turned the war into a fight against slavery and opened the way for Black soldiers to enlist. Lincoln removed McClellan weeks later for failing to pursue Lee's beaten army.

bat-little-bighorn.why: The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie had guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota, but an army expedition led by Custer confirmed gold there in 1874 and prospectors poured in. The government ordered all Lakota onto reservations by early 1876, declared those who stayed away hostile and sent three army columns after them.
bat-little-bighorn.impact: News of the defeat reached the East during the celebrations of the nation's centennial and caused outrage. Congress seized the Black Hills in 1877, Crazy Horse surrendered that year and Sitting Bull fled to Canada. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the land had been taken illegally, but the Sioux refused the money offered.

bat-battle-of-britain-day.why: After France fell in June 1940, Hitler planned an invasion of Britain codenamed Operation Sea Lion, which first required control of the skies. The RAF's radar chain and control system let it meet raids efficiently, and in early September the Luftwaffe turned its attacks on London, partly in reprisal for British raids on Berlin.
bat-battle-of-britain-day.impact: With Britain undefeated, Hitler turned east and invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, though the night Blitz on British cities continued until May. Britain survived to become the base for the bombing campaign and the D-Day landings, and 15 September is still marked each year as Battle of Britain Day.

bat-battle-of-the-bulge.why: After D-Day the Allies raced across France, but their supply lines were stretched thin. Hitler gambled on a winter offensive through the hilly, wooded Ardennes, the same route his armies had used in 1940, aiming to split the Allied armies, recapture the port of Antwerp and force a negotiated peace in the west.
bat-battle-of-the-bulge.impact: It was the largest battle the US Army fought in the war, with around nineteen thousand Americans killed. Germany lost tanks, aircraft and reserves it could not replace, leaving it far weaker in the west. The Allies crossed the Rhine in March 1945, and Germany surrendered in May.

bat-iwo-jima-flag.why: Iwo Jima lay roughly halfway between American bases in the Mariana Islands and Tokyo, and Japanese fighters there could intercept B-29 bombers on their way to Japan. Under General Kuribayashi, the defenders had dug miles of tunnels and bunkers into the island. The flag was raised on Mount Suribachi, its highest point.
bat-iwo-jima-flag.impact: Joe Rosenthal's photograph won the Pulitzer Prize and was used to promote war bonds, and three of the six men in it were killed later in the battle. Almost seven thousand US Marines died and nearly all the Japanese garrison was killed, but damaged B-29s went on to make more than two thousand emergency landings there.

bat-bay-of-pigs.why: After Fidel Castro took power in 1959, he nationalised American-owned businesses and drew closer to Moscow. Under Eisenhower the CIA began training Cuban exiles in Guatemala to overthrow him. Kennedy inherited the plan and approved it, but limited American involvement to keep it deniable, and early air strikes failed to destroy Castro's air force.
bat-bay-of-pigs.impact: More than a thousand invaders were captured and later freed in exchange for about $53 million worth of food and medicine. Kennedy publicly took responsibility, CIA director Allen Dulles was forced out, and the administration launched a covert campaign of sabotage and assassination plots against Castro known as Operation Mongoose.

bat-desert-storm.why: Iraq came out of its long war with Iran deeply in debt and accused Kuwait of driving down oil prices and stealing oil from a shared field. After the invasion, the UN authorised force if Iraq did not withdraw by 15 January 1991, and a US-led coalition of dozens of countries massed troops in Saudi Arabia.
bat-desert-storm.impact: Retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells on fire. Saddam stayed in power and crushed Shia and Kurdish uprisings, leading to no-fly zones, years of sanctions and weapons inspections that set the stage for the 2003 invasion. The war also showcased precision-guided bombs and stealth aircraft.

ppl-henry-viii.why: Henry was the second son of Henry VII, who had seized the crown at Bosworth in 1485 and married Elizabeth of York to unite the rival houses of Lancaster and York. As a younger son he was not expected to rule, and he grew up a talented athlete, musician and scholar.
ppl-henry-viii.impact: He dissolved England's monasteries and transferred their vast lands and wealth to the crown, and he built up the navy, including warships such as the Mary Rose. All three of his surviving children, Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I, became monarchs, and the Church of England he created still exists today.

ppl-jane-austen.why: Austen was born at Steventon rectory in Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a clergyman, George Austen. Her father's large library and the family's love of reading and amateur theatricals fed her early writing, and her closest companion was her sister Cassandra. Two of her brothers became admirals in the Royal Navy.
ppl-jane-austen.impact: Her brother Henry revealed her name to the public after her death, when Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published. Her use of free indirect speech, letting the narrator slip into a character's thoughts, influenced generations of novelists. Her novels inspired countless film and television adaptations, and since 2017 she has appeared on the Bank of England's ten-pound note.

ppl-marie-antoinette-executed.why: Her marriage was arranged to seal an alliance between France and Austria, and many French people distrusted her as a foreigner. The Diamond Necklace Affair of 1785 wrecked her reputation though she was innocent, the royal family's failed flight to Varennes in 1791 destroyed trust in them, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
ppl-marie-antoinette-executed.impact: Her death came during the Reign of Terror, in which thousands were executed. Her young son died in prison in 1795, while her daughter was the only member of the family imprisoned in the Temple to survive. After the Bourbons returned, her remains were reburied in the royal basilica of Saint-Denis in 1815.

ppl-charles-dickens.why: Dickens was born in Portsmouth, where his father worked as a clerk in the navy pay office. Because the family was often short of money, he had little formal schooling, and he later worked as a law clerk and a shorthand reporter in Parliament. His early sketches, signed Boz, led to the hugely popular Pickwick Papers.
ppl-charles-dickens.impact: His novels exposed the cruelty of workhouses, debtors' prisons, schools and the courts, and helped push public opinion towards reform. A Christmas Carol did much to shape the modern Christmas of family feasts and generosity. His public reading tours drew huge crowds in Britain and America, and he was buried in Westminster Abbey.

ppl-nikola-tesla.why: Tesla was born to a Serbian family in Smiljan, then part of the Austrian Empire and now in Croatia, where his father was an Orthodox priest. He studied engineering at Graz and worked for Edison's company in Paris before crossing to New York in 1884 with ideas for a motor driven by alternating current.
ppl-nikola-tesla.impact: George Westinghouse bought his alternating-current patents, and the rivalry with Edison's direct current became known as the war of the currents. Alternating current lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and was used for the great hydroelectric plant at Niagara Falls. Shortly after his death, the US Supreme Court invalidated a key Marconi radio patent.

ppl-pablo-picasso.why: Picasso was born in Málaga, the son of José Ruiz Blasco, a painter and art teacher who trained him from an early age. The family moved to A Coruña and then Barcelona, where the young artist mixed with avant-garde circles, and in 1904 he settled in Paris, the centre of the art world.
ppl-pablo-picasso.impact: His painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon broke sharply with traditional perspective and opened the way to Cubism, and he and Braque pioneered collage. He also worked in sculpture, ceramics and printmaking, and influenced almost every major movement of the century. Guernica was sent to Spain only in 1981, after democracy returned, as he had wished.

ppl-elizabeth-ii.why: Elizabeth was born in London, the first child of the Duke and Duchess of York, and was third in line to the throne at birth. Nobody expected her to become queen, because her uncle Edward was expected to marry and have children. She was educated at home alongside her younger sister, Margaret.
ppl-elizabeth-ii.impact: During the Second World War she trained as a mechanic in the women's Auxiliary Territorial Service. Her televised coronation in 1953 helped make television a fixture in British homes. She oversaw the end of empire and the growth of the Commonwealth, and fifteen prime ministers served her, from Winston Churchill to Liz Truss.

ppl-thatcher-prime-minister.why: Thatcher was a grocer's daughter from Grantham who trained as a chemist and a barrister, served as education secretary and won the Conservative leadership in 1975. James Callaghan's Labour government lost a vote of confidence by a single vote in March 1979, and the Conservatives won the general election that May.
ppl-thatcher-prime-minister.impact: She was Britain's first woman prime minister. Her government let council tenants buy their homes, curbed trade-union powers and deregulated the City of London in the Big Bang of 1986. The deeply unpopular poll tax sparked riots in 1990, and later that year her own party forced her from office.

ppl-john-lennon-shot.why: After the Beatles split in 1970, Lennon settled in New York and fought a long battle against deportation by the Nixon administration. He then spent five years away from music raising his son Sean, and had just returned with the album Double Fantasy. Chapman, a security guard from Hawaii, had become obsessed with him.
ppl-john-lennon-shot.impact: Double Fantasy topped the charts and won the Grammy for Album of the Year. At Yoko Ono's request, millions around the world observed ten minutes of silence six days after his death. Chapman pleaded guilty to murder and was sentenced to twenty years to life, and he has repeatedly been denied parole.

ppl-obama-inaugurated.why: Born in Honolulu, Obama became the first Black president of the Harvard Law Review and later an Illinois state senator. A speech at the 2004 Democratic convention made him a national figure. He beat Hillary Clinton in a long primary race and defeated John McCain weeks after the collapse of Lehman Brothers.
ppl-obama-inaugurated.impact: He became the first African American president of the United States. His government passed a large economic stimulus package and the Affordable Care Act, which extended health insurance to millions. He ended the US combat mission in Iraq, approved the 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden and joined the Paris climate agreement.

tec-ferris-wheel.why: Chicago's World's Columbian Exposition marked four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas, and the Eiffel Tower had been the star of the 1889 Paris fair. The fair's chief architect, Daniel Burnham, challenged American engineers to produce something original. Ferris, a bridge builder and steel inspector from Pittsburgh, answered with a giant revolving wheel.
tec-ferris-wheel.impact: After the fair the wheel was taken down, rebuilt in Chicago and then moved to the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, before being demolished with dynamite in 1906. It inspired observation wheels around the world, such as Vienna's Riesenrad and the London Eye, and Ferris's name became the everyday word for them.

tec-model-t.why: Early cars were mostly hand-built and expensive, playthings for the wealthy. Henry Ford wanted a simple, tough car that ordinary families could afford and repair themselves. The Model T used light but strong vanadium steel, sat high enough to cope with rough country roads, and went on sale for around $850.
tec-model-t.impact: The moving assembly line cut the time to build a chassis from about twelve hours to roughly an hour and a half, and Ford's five-dollar day doubled many workers' pay. Mass car ownership changed American life, encouraging paved roads, petrol stations and suburbs, and other industries copied Ford's methods of mass production.

tec-first-tank-battle.why: By 1915 the Western Front had become a deadlock of trenches, barbed wire and machine guns that slaughtered attacking infantry. Officers such as Ernest Swinton proposed armoured vehicles that could cross no-man's-land, and Winston Churchill, then at the Admiralty, backed a committee to develop them. They were first used at Flers-Courcelette during the Battle of the Somme.
tec-first-tank-battle.impact: Tanks improved quickly, and hundreds were used together at Cambrai in 1917 and Amiens in 1918. Between the wars thinkers such as J. F. C. Fuller and Heinz Guderian worked out how fast-moving armour could be combined with aircraft and infantry, ideas Germany put into practice in the Second World War.

tec-walkman.why: Sony already made the Pressman, a small cassette recorder used by journalists, and the compact cassette had become a popular music format. Co-founder Akio Morita backed the idea of a player without a recording function or speaker, even though many in the company doubted anyone would buy it.
tec-walkman.impact: For the first time people could carry their own soundtrack through streets, trains and gyms, and some critics worried it made them antisocial. It was first sold in some countries under names such as Soundabout and Stowaway. Sony followed with the Discman, and the Walkman paved the way for the iPod.

tec-compact-disc.why: Philips had been working on optical discs read by lasers, while Sony was developing digital audio recording, and the two firms agreed a common standard in 1980. They settled on a disc 12 centimetres across that could hold about 74 minutes of music. The first players and discs went on sale in Japan.
tec-compact-disc.impact: Dire Straits' Brothers in Arms became one of the first albums to sell a million copies on CD, and record companies reissued their back catalogues, fuelling a sales boom in the 1990s. The CD-ROM put software and encyclopedias on disc, but copying CDs to MP3 files later helped bring on file sharing and streaming.

tec-game-boy.why: Gunpei Yokoi had already created Nintendo's Game and Watch handhelds, and he favoured cheap, proven technology used in new ways. The Nintendo Entertainment System had made Nintendo the leader in home video games, and the company wanted a portable machine with interchangeable cartridges. In North America it came bundled with Tetris.
tec-game-boy.impact: Rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear had colour screens but drained batteries quickly, and the Game Boy outsold them easily. It was followed by the Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS, and the Pokémon games first released on it grew into one of the biggest entertainment franchises in the world.

tec-first-text-message.why: The GSM digital mobile standard included a Short Message Service, limited to 160 characters, which was mainly intended for networks to send notices to customers. Neil Papworth, a young engineer working on Vodafone's network, was testing the system when he sent the message Merry Christmas.
tec-first-text-message.impact: Nokia launched phones that could send texts the following year, and once customers could text people on other networks, usage soared. Predictive text and a whole shorthand of abbreviations followed. Twitter's original 140-character limit was based on the size of a text message, and in 2021 the first SMS was auctioned as an NFT for charity.

tec-google-founded.why: Larry Page and Sergey Brin met as PhD students at Stanford, where they built a search engine called BackRub. Early search engines ranked pages mainly by how often keywords appeared, which was easily gamed. Investor Andy Bechtolsheim made his cheque out to Google Inc. before the company legally existed, so they had to incorporate it.
tec-google-founded.impact: Advertising linked to search terms made the company enormously profitable, and it went public in 2004. Google launched Gmail and Maps, bought YouTube and developed the Android phone system, and in 2006 major dictionaries added google as a verb. In 2015 it reorganised under a new parent company, Alphabet.

tec-facebook-launch.why: Harvard's dormitories printed directories of students' photos, known as face books. Mark Zuckerberg, a second-year student, had already caused trouble with Facemash, a site that compared students' pictures. He launched TheFacebook from his dormitory with fellow students including Eduardo Saverin, Dustin Moskovitz and Chris Hughes.
tec-facebook-launch.impact: The News Feed, added in 2006, changed how people shared their lives online. Facebook bought Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014, and it was used to organise protests during the Arab Spring. The Cambridge Analytica data scandal of 2018 brought heavy scrutiny, and the company renamed itself Meta in 2021.

tec-youtube-first-video.why: YouTube was founded by three former PayPal employees, Chad Hurley, Steve Chen and Jawed Karim. Sharing video online was then awkward, with large files and incompatible players, but broadband was spreading quickly. The site played videos in the web browser using Flash. The first upload, Me at the Zoo, was filmed at San Diego Zoo.
tec-youtube-first-video.impact: Google paid $1.65 billion in stock for the site. It turned ordinary people into stars and made video-making a career, and it became a major home for music videos, tutorials and news footage. By the late 2010s more than five hundred hours of video were being uploaded every minute.

exp-mont-blanc.why: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps, and many local people feared its glaciers and crevasses. Saussure first offered his reward in 1760 after visiting Chamonix, but several attempts failed. Jacques Balmat was a crystal hunter and chamois hunter, and Michel-Gabriel Paccard was the village doctor.
exp-mont-blanc.impact: The two men's roles were long disputed, as Balmat's version, popularised by Alexandre Dumas, played down Paccard's part until historians restored it. Chamonix became a centre for tourists and climbers, the Alpine Club was founded in London in 1857, and the golden age of Alpine climbing ended with the first ascent of the Matterhorn in 1865.

exp-nellie-bly.why: Nellie Bly, the pen name of Elizabeth Cochrane, had made her name by faking insanity to expose conditions inside a New York women's asylum. Her editors at first said only a man could make the trip, but she insisted and set off with a single small bag. A rival magazine sent Elizabeth Bisland racing in the opposite direction.
exp-nellie-bly.impact: She completed the trip in seventy-two days, and the World ran a contest for readers to guess her time. Her record was beaten within months by George Francis Train. Bly later took over her late husband's manufacturing company and reported from the Eastern Front during the First World War.

exp-bleriot-channel.why: Wilbur Wright's demonstrations in France in 1908 had shown how far behind European aviators were, and the Daily Mail offered a prize for the first flight across the English Channel. Blériot had crashed many of his earlier designs and was still nursing a burned foot. His rival Hubert Latham had come down in the sea just days earlier.
exp-bleriot-channel.impact: The flight lasted about thirty-seven minutes and brought Blériot a flood of orders for his monoplane, which became one of the most popular aircraft of the period. His company later took over SPAD, whose fighters flew in the First World War, when aircraft first changed the face of warfare.

exp-alcock-brown.why: The Daily Mail first offered its prize in 1913, but the First World War put the challenge on hold. Alcock and Brown had both flown in the war and both had been taken prisoner. Their Vimy was a modified bomber, and they raced several rival teams gathered in Newfoundland, weeks after a US Navy flying boat crossed in stages.
exp-alcock-brown.impact: Both men were knighted by King George V within days of landing. Alcock was killed in a flying accident in France just six months later. Regular passenger flights across the Atlantic did not begin until 1939, and a statue of the two airmen now stands at Heathrow Airport.

exp-lascaux.why: The cave lies in the Vézère valley of the Dordogne in south-western France, near the town of Montignac. A rockfall had sealed its entrance for thousands of years, which kept the paintings in remarkable condition. Teenagers investigating a hole left by a fallen tree found the passage, and the priest and prehistorian Henri Breuil soon examined it.
exp-lascaux.impact: After it closed in 1963, the cave suffered further outbreaks of mould and fungus that scientists still struggle to control. Exact copies opened nearby in 1983 and 2016, and the decorated caves of the valley became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. The paintings changed views of how sophisticated Ice Age people were.

exp-kon-tiki.why: Thor Heyerdahl, a Norwegian explorer, had lived on the Marquesas Islands and believed that Polynesia had been settled from South America, against the view of most scholars that settlers came from Asia. Experts warned that a balsa raft would become waterlogged and sink. He and five crew set out from Callao in Peru.
exp-kon-tiki.impact: The film of the voyage won an Academy Award, and the raft is displayed in the Kon-Tiki Museum in Oslo. Later DNA studies showed that Polynesians came mainly from Asia by way of the Pacific islands, though a 2020 study found signs of contact with Native Americans around eight hundred years ago.

exp-sound-barrier.why: During the Second World War fighter pilots diving at high speed found their controls stiffening or locking as they neared the speed of sound, and some believed the barrier could not be crossed. In 1946 Geoffrey de Havilland Jr. was killed testing a fast jet. The rocket-powered Bell X-1 was shaped like a rifle bullet and dropped from a bomber.
exp-sound-barrier.impact: The flight opened the way to supersonic fighters and to rocket planes such as the X-15, which flew to the edge of space. Yeager himself passed twice the speed of sound in 1953. The passenger jet Concorde entered service in 1976, and Tom Wolfe's book The Right Stuff made Yeager a legend.

exp-terracotta-army.why: Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BCE and became its first emperor, standardising its writing, coins and weights and measures. Work on his vast tomb near modern Xi'an began when he became king of Qin as a boy. In March 1974 farmers digging a well came across fragments of clay figures.
exp-terracotta-army.impact: Three main pits are thought to hold around eight thousand figures, but excavation is slow because the original painted colours begin to fade and flake within minutes of exposure to air. Touring exhibitions of the warriors have drawn huge crowds around the world, and the site has transformed understanding of the Qin dynasty.

exp-titanic-wreck.why: The Titanic sank in 1912 with the loss of about fifteen hundred lives, but it lay nearly four kilometres down, and the position given in its distress calls was inaccurate. Earlier searches had failed. Ballard's American team worked with France's ocean research institute, which first swept the area with sonar.
exp-titanic-wreck.impact: Ballard returned in 1986 in the submersible Alvin, and later expeditions raised thousands of artefacts, despite objections that the site was a grave. The wreck gained UNESCO protection in 2012, James Cameron's 1997 film used real footage of it, and bacteria are steadily eating away its steel.

exp-baumgartner-jump.why: Felix Baumgartner was an Austrian skydiver and BASE jumper. The Red Bull Stratos project set out to beat the record set by US Air Force officer Joseph Kittinger, who jumped from about 31 kilometres in 1960. Kittinger, then in his eighties, served as an adviser and spoke to Baumgartner by radio during the ascent from Roswell, New Mexico.
exp-baumgartner-jump.impact: Baumgartner became the first person to break the sound barrier in freefall without a vehicle. Data from the jump fed into research on pressure suits and escape systems for high-altitude flight and spaceflight. In 2014 Google executive Alan Eustace jumped from even higher, about 41 kilometres, with far less publicity.

spc-uranus-discovered.why: William Herschel was a German-born musician who settled in Bath and became fascinated by astronomy. He built his own reflecting telescopes, which were better than most professional instruments of the day, and with his sister Caroline he was methodically surveying the night sky star by star when he spotted the object.
spc-uranus-discovered.impact: King George III gave Herschel a royal pension, letting him give up music for astronomy, and he went on to discover two of Uranus's moons. Irregularities in Uranus's orbit later led astronomers to predict and find Neptune in 1846. Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus, flying past in 1986.

spc-pluto-discovered.why: Percival Lowell founded an observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, and believed that unexplained wobbles in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune meant another planet lay beyond them. Clyde Tombaugh, a Kansas farm boy, got the job after sending the observatory drawings made with his homemade telescope, and found Pluto by comparing photographs taken nights apart.
spc-pluto-discovered.impact: Pluto proved far too small to disturb Neptune, and Lowell's calculations turned out to be mistaken. Its moon Charon was found in 1978, and from 1992 many more icy bodies were discovered in the Kuiper belt. NASA's New Horizons probe flew past Pluto in 2015 carrying some of Tombaugh's ashes.

spc-glenn-orbit.why: The Soviet Union had already sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit in April 1961 and Gherman Titov on a flight lasting a full day, while the United States had managed only two short suborbital hops. Glenn's Friendship 7 mission had been postponed many times before his Atlas rocket finally lifted off.
spc-glenn-orbit.impact: His flight of three orbits, lasting just under five hours, restored American confidence in the space race and was celebrated with a ticker-tape parade in New York. It built support for the Gemini and Apollo programmes. Glenn later served as a US senator for Ohio for twenty-four years.

spc-we-choose-the-moon.why: Shaken by Gagarin's orbit and the Bay of Pigs fiasco, Kennedy wanted a goal where the United States could beat the Soviets. NASA was building its new Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, and he gave the speech at Rice University while touring the new space facilities. Privately, he worried about the enormous cost.
spc-we-choose-the-moon.impact: NASA's budget rose to over four percent of federal spending in the mid-1960s, and around four hundred thousand people worked on Apollo at its peak. The line about choosing to go to the Moon not because it is easy but because it is hard became one of the most quoted in American politics.

spc-pathfinder.why: No spacecraft had landed on Mars since the Viking missions of 1976, and the expensive Mars Observer orbiter had been lost in 1993. NASA's new Discovery programme promised smaller, cheaper missions under the slogan faster, better, cheaper. Pathfinder landed on 4 July 1997 in an ancient flood channel called Ares Vallis.
spc-pathfinder.impact: Sojourner was the first wheeled rover to explore another planet. The airbag landing system was reused for the Spirit and Opportunity rovers in 2004, and the mission paved the way for larger rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance. The lander was renamed the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.

spc-first-space-tourist.why: Earlier visitors such as the Japanese journalist Toyohiro Akiyama and the British chemist Helen Sharman had flown with Soviet crews, but their seats were paid for by sponsors. Tito first arranged to visit the Russian space station Mir, but when Mir was brought down in 2001 the company Space Adventures switched his trip to a Soyuz flight to the ISS.
spc-first-space-tourist.impact: Space Adventures went on to send several more paying visitors to the space station, including Anousheh Ansari, the first female space tourist, and Charles Simonyi, who flew twice. In 2021 Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic began suborbital tourist flights, and the Inspiration4 mission took the first all-civilian crew into orbit.

spc-columbia-disaster.why: Columbia, the oldest orbiter, was on a sixteen-day science mission. Foam had struck orbiters on earlier flights without disaster, so NASA had come to treat it as a routine maintenance issue rather than a safety threat, and engineers' requests for images of the damaged wing were turned down. All seven crew died over Texas.
spc-columbia-disaster.impact: The investigation board found that NASA's culture was as much to blame as the foam itself. When flights resumed in 2005, crews used a boom to inspect the heat shield in orbit and trained to make repairs. The last Shuttle mission flew in 2011, after the space station was largely complete.

spc-falcon-heavy.why: Falcon Heavy was essentially three Falcon 9 first stages strapped together, and SpaceX had already shown it could land Falcon 9 boosters for reuse. After years of delays, Elon Musk warned there was a good chance the rocket would explode, so instead of a valuable payload he sent his own red Tesla Roadster with a dummy in a spacesuit.
spc-falcon-heavy.impact: The central booster missed its drone ship and hit the sea, but the launch proved that a reusable heavy rocket could cut costs. Falcon Heavy went on to carry satellites for military and commercial customers and to launch NASA's Psyche probe in 2023 and Europa Clipper mission in 2024.

spc-crew-dragon.why: After 2011 NASA was paying Russia tens of millions of dollars per seat to fly its astronauts. Under its Commercial Crew Program, NASA chose SpaceX and Boeing in 2014 to build new spacecraft, and SpaceX's Dragon capsule had already been carrying cargo to the station since 2012. The astronauts were Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley.
spc-crew-dragon.impact: The capsule splashed down safely in the Gulf of Mexico in August, and regular crew rotation flights began that November. Crew Dragon also opened the way for private missions such as Inspiration4 and Axiom's flights to the station, and it brought home the crew of Boeing's troubled first crewed Starliner flight in 2025.

spc-ingenuity.why: Mars's air is only about one percent as dense as Earth's at sea level, so engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory had to build a helicopter with very light, fast-spinning twin rotors. It was a technology demonstration. Perseverance had landed in Jezero Crater in February 2021, and the take-off site was named Wright Brothers Field.
spc-ingenuity.impact: Ingenuity was planned for just five test flights in thirty days, but it became an aerial scout helping plan the rover's route. Its mission ended in January 2024 when a rotor blade was damaged. It proved powered flight was possible on another world, encouraging plans for future Mars helicopters and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft for Titan.
